topics.h: Is there a magic trick that turns a tiny seed into a mango tree overnight? Let's find out!
p: The lesson 'A Bottle of Dew' is a story about wanting quick success and learning the value of hard work.
A shortcut promises fast results with little effort; hard work means steady effort over time.
To understand a story, ask: Who is in it? What do they want? What problem do they face? How does it end?
The moral of a story is the lesson it teaches. We find it by looking at what happens to the characters because of their choices.
Read every question carefully and look back at the passage for the exact words that prove your answer.

ex.q: Read this passage: Meera wanted the best mangoes in the village. Her friend Kabir said, "Just buy a magic powder and the tree will fruit overnight!" Meera shook her head. Every morning she watered her little tree, pulled out weeds and added compost. Two summers later, her tree gave sweet, golden mangoes, and she shared them with everyone. What lesson does the story teach?
st: Meera's goal: to grow the best mangoes.
Kabir offers a shortcut: a 'magic powder'.
Meera chooses steady work: watering, weeding and adding compost every day.
Result: after two summers, her tree gives sweet mangoes.
So the story shows that patient hard work brings real results.
ex.a: Patient, steady hard work brings real success; shortcuts rarely do.

topics.rl: Practising cricket in the nets every evening, or revising a little every day before exams, works better than hoping for a last-minute trick.

topics.h: Words like 'honest', 'patient' and 'greedy' are tiny labels that tell us what a person is really like inside.
p: Values are good qualities that guide how we behave: honesty, patience, kindness, hard work, sharing.
Synonyms are words with similar meanings: hard-working = diligent; patient = calm while waiting.
Antonyms are words with opposite meanings: honest ↔ dishonest, patient ↔ impatient, generous ↔ selfish.
The prefixes 'un-', 'im-' and 'dis-' can make opposites: kind → unkind, patient → impatient, honest → dishonest.
We judge characters by what they say and do, not just by what they are called.

ex.q: Think it through: Arjun finds a ₹100 note in the school corridor and hands it to his teacher. Which value does he show, and what is its opposite?
st: Arjun does not keep money that isn't his.
Returning lost things shows honesty.
Adding 'dis-' to 'honest' gives its opposite.
ex.a: Honesty; the opposite word is 'dishonest'.

topics.rl: When you return a friend's lost pencil box or wait calmly in the lunch queue, you are showing values in action.

topics.t: Telling a story in the simple past
topics.h: Most stories begin with 'Once upon a time...' and then the verbs travel back in time!
p: Stories usually use the simple past tense because they tell about things that already happened.
Regular verbs add -ed or -d: walk → walked, water → watered, smile → smiled.
Irregular verbs change in their own way: go → went, buy → bought, give → gave, see → saw.
Negative: did not + base verb ('She did not buy the powder', not 'did not bought').
Question: Did + subject + base verb ('Did Meera work hard?').

ex.q: Think it through: Change to the simple past: 'Meera waters the tree and Kabir buys a powder.'
st: 'waters' is regular, so add -ed: watered.
'buys' is irregular: buy → bought.
Put the sentence together.
ex.a: Meera watered the tree and Kabir bought a powder.

topics.rl: When you tell your family what happened at school today, you naturally use the past tense: 'We played kho-kho.'

topics.h: What happens when an old animal story learns to rhyme? It becomes a fable in verse!
p: 'The Raven and the Fox' is a fable told as a poem: a clever fox tricks a bird by praising it.
A fable is a short story, often with animals that talk, which teaches a moral (a lesson).
'In verse' means written in lines of poetry, often with rhythm and rhyme, instead of ordinary paragraphs (prose).
A group of lines in a poem is called a stanza. Words that end with the same sound, like 'tight' and 'delight', are rhyming words.
Many famous fables come from Aesop (ancient Greece) and from the Panchatantra (ancient India).

ex.q: Read this original poem: A myna sat upon a tree, / A roti in her beak held tight. / A jackal called, "O bird so fair, / Your song must be a pure delight!" / She sang out loud — the roti fell; / He grabbed it quick and ran from sight. / Now Myna knows that honeyed words / Can hide a plan that isn't right. Which words rhyme, and what is the moral?
st: Look at the last word of each line: tree, tight, fair, delight, fell, sight, words, right.
'tight', 'delight', 'sight' and 'right' all end with the same '-ight' sound.
The myna lost her roti because she believed the jackal's sweet words.
So the lesson is about not trusting flattery.
ex.a: Rhyming words: tight, delight, sight, right. Moral: don't be fooled by sweet words of flattery.

topics.rl: Panchatantra tales, Jataka tales and cartoon fables on TV all teach a moral through animal characters.

topics.t: Flattery: sweet words with a hidden plan
topics.h: If someone suddenly says you're the best singer in the whole universe, should you smile — or check your tiffin?
p: Flattery is praise that is too much and not sincere, usually given to get something from the person.
Honest praise is true and fair: 'Your drawing has lovely colours.' Flattery is over the top: 'You are the greatest artist who ever lived!'
Word family: flatter (verb), flattery (noun), flatterer (a person who flatters).
'Honeyed words' and 'sweet talk' are phrases for pleasant words that may hide a trick. The idiom 'to butter someone up' (in Hindi, 'makkhan lagana') means to flatter them.
A wise person enjoys kind words but still thinks: 'Is this true? Why is this person saying it?'

ex.q: Think it through: Raju tells Aman, 'You're the smartest boy in the whole world! Can I copy your homework?' Is this honest praise or flattery?
st: The praise is far too big to be true.
Raju wants something right after praising: to copy homework.
Too-big praise + a hidden purpose = flattery.
ex.a: It is flattery, because the praise is exaggerated and is used to get something.

topics.rl: Advertisements and some online messages flatter you ('Lucky winner! You are special!') to make you click or buy — so think before you trust.

topics.h: The jackal didn't just say 'nice bird' — he piled on adjectives! Let's learn how to compare with them.
p: An adjective describes a noun: a clever jackal, a hungry myna, a tall tree.
Adjectives have three degrees: positive (sweet), comparative (sweeter) and superlative (sweetest).
Use the comparative (+ 'than') for two things: 'The fox is cleverer than the raven.' Use the superlative (+ 'the') for three or more: 'the tallest tree'.
Short adjectives add -er/-est (tall, taller, tallest); long ones use more/most (beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful).
Some are irregular: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; many, more, most.

ex.q: Think it through: Fill in: 'Of all the birds in the garden, the peacock is the ___ (colourful).'
st: 'Of all the birds' compares more than two, so we need the superlative.
'Colourful' is a long adjective, so it uses 'most'.
Superlatives take 'the' before them.
ex.a: the most colourful

topics.rl: Shopping and sports talk is full of comparisons: 'This mango is sweeter', 'Rohit is the fastest runner in our class.'

topics.h: A monkey, a pair of spectacles and one smart girl — what could go wrong? (Everything, and then everything goes right!)
p: 'Rama to the Rescue' is a humorous folk tale in which quick thinking saves the day.
A folk tale is a traditional story passed down by people telling it aloud, often from grandparents to children.
Humour comes from funny situations, surprising twists, silly characters and sound words like 'Plop!'
Words that imitate sounds (plop, buzz, splash, crash) are called onomatopoeia.
When reading, notice the problem, the turning point (where things change) and how the problem is solved.

ex.q: Read: At a busy railway station, a cheeky monkey snatched Dadaji's spectacles and leapt onto the roof of a tea stall. People shouted and waved, but the monkey only chattered. Little Lata stayed calm. She held up a banana. Plop! The monkey dropped the spectacles into Dadaji's lap and grabbed the fruit. Everyone laughed and clapped. What was the problem, and how was it solved?
st: Problem: the monkey took Dadaji's spectacles.
Shouting and waving did not help.
Turning point: Lata calmly held up a banana.
Solution: the monkey dropped the spectacles to grab the fruit.
ex.a: The monkey stole Dadaji's spectacles; Lata got them back by offering it a banana.

topics.rl: Monkeys at temples and stations in many Indian towns really do snatch things — and people often trade fruit to get them back!

topics.h: When something goes wrong, do you panic like a pressure cooker or think like a detective?
p: Presence of mind means staying calm and thinking quickly in a sudden or difficult situation.
A person with presence of mind is quick-witted, calm and resourceful (good at finding ways to solve problems).
Useful phrases: 'keep a cool head' (stay calm), 'think on your feet' (think quickly), 'at one's wits' end' (not knowing what to do).
Panic usually makes problems worse; a calm, clever idea often fixes them.
In an emergency, presence of mind also means telling a trusted adult quickly or calling helplines like 112.

ex.q: Think it through: During a class picnic, the bus driver says the road ahead is blocked. Students start crying. Priya asks, 'Is there another road? Can we inform our teacher and parents?' What does Priya show?
st: Others panic and cry.
Priya stays calm.
She thinks of a practical solution and informs adults.
Calm + quick thinking = presence of mind.
ex.a: Priya shows presence of mind: she stays calm and thinks of sensible next steps.

topics.rl: Firefighters, doctors in emergency rooms and even goalkeepers need presence of mind every day.

topics.h: Punctuation marks are the traffic signals of writing — they tell readers when to stop, pause, ask or shout!
p: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop (.), question mark (?) or exclamation mark (!).
Speech marks (quotation marks " ") go around the exact words someone says: Lata said, "Wait, I have an idea."
Put a comma after 'said' before the spoken words, and keep the end punctuation of the speech inside the closing speech marks.
Commas separate items in a list: bananas, apples and guavas. An apostrophe shows possession (Dadaji's spectacles) or missing letters (don't = do not).
Proper nouns like names of people, places and days always begin with a capital letter: Lata, Jaipur, Monday.

ex.q: Think it through: Punctuate this: lata said dont worry dadaji
st: Start with a capital: Lata.
Add a comma after 'said'.
Open speech marks and use a capital letter for the first spoken word: "Don't...
'dont' needs an apostrophe: don't.
Dadaji is a name, so capital D, and close with a full stop inside the speech marks.
ex.a: Lata said, "Don't worry, Dadaji."

topics.rl: Chat messages, posters and signboards all need correct punctuation — 'Let's eat, Grandma!' is very different from 'Let's eat Grandma!'

topics.h: A noisy cricket fan and a quiet painter — can they be best friends? Let's read and see!
p: 'The Unlikely Best Friends' is about a friendship between two people who seem very different.
'Unlikely' means not expected. An unlikely friendship is one people would not expect.
Good friends can have different hobbies, habits and backgrounds; what matters is respect, trust and care.
Characters change in a story. Notice how their feelings at the start differ from their feelings at the end.
Look for clues in what characters say and do to understand their nature (character traits).

ex.q: Read: Tara loved noisy cricket matches. Bholu, her new neighbour, loved quiet painting. "We have nothing in common," Tara grumbled. Then Tara hurt her ankle and had to sit at home for a week. Bholu came over with his paints and taught her to paint the sunset. On Sports Day, when Bholu was nervous before his race, Tara cheered louder than anyone. How did Tara's feelings about Bholu change?
st: At first Tara said, 'We have nothing in common.'
When she was hurt, Bholu helped her by teaching her to paint.
Later, Tara cheered loudly for Bholu at Sports Day.
So she went from thinking they were too different to being his supportive friend.
ex.a: At first she thought they had nothing in common, but after Bholu helped her, she became his caring friend.

topics.rl: Your best friend may love maths while you love music — differences can make a friendship more fun.

topics.h: Some of the best stories are tiny true-life moments — just a few lines that show who a person really was.
p: An anecdote is a short, interesting story about a real person or a real event.
Anecdotes are usually told in the past tense and often show a person's character: their wit, kindness or courage.
Many anecdotes are told about Emperor Akbar and Birbal, a witty member of his court. These stories have been told and retold for centuries as popular folk tales.
An anecdote has a setting, a small problem or question, and a clever or surprising ending.
A friendship can be 'unlikely' when two people are very different in age, position or nature, yet value each other.

ex.q: Read this anecdote, told in our own words: One day Akbar drew a line on the floor and said, 'Make this line shorter without rubbing out any part of it.' The courtiers were puzzled. Birbal simply drew a longer line beside it. Now Akbar's line looked shorter! What does this anecdote show about Birbal?
st: The problem: shorten a line without touching it.
Others could not think of a way.
Birbal changed the comparison by drawing a longer line next to it.
This shows quick, clever thinking.
ex.a: It shows that Birbal was witty and could think in a clever, unusual way.

topics.rl: Your grandparents' stories about 'the day the first TV came to our street' are family anecdotes!

topics.h: Friendship, Birbal, team, palace — all nouns! But each one is a different kind. Let's sort them.
p: A noun names a person, place, animal, thing or idea.
Common nouns are general names (girl, city, river). Proper nouns are particular names and begin with capitals (Tara, Agra, Yamuna).
Collective nouns name a group as one: a team of players, a flock of birds, a herd of cattle, a swarm of bees, a bunch of grapes.
Abstract nouns name feelings, qualities or ideas we cannot see or touch: friendship, kindness, courage, honesty, wisdom.
Many abstract nouns are made with suffixes: friend → friendship, kind → kindness, brave → bravery, wise → wisdom.

ex.q: Think it through: Find the kinds of nouns in: 'Birbal's wisdom amazed the crowd in Agra.'
st: Birbal and Agra are particular names → proper nouns.
Wisdom is an idea we can't touch → abstract noun.
Crowd names a group of people → collective noun.
ex.a: Proper: Birbal, Agra; abstract: wisdom; collective: crowd.

topics.rl: Your school (proper noun), your class team (collective noun) and your friendship (abstract noun) are all around you!

topics.h: If you could write a wish for the kind of friend you want to be, what would it say?
p: 'A Friend's Prayer' is a poem in which the speaker wishes to be a good, true friend.
A prayer is a humble wish or request. Lines starting with 'Let me be...' express such wishes.
The rhyme scheme shows which lines rhyme. We give the same letter to lines that rhyme: AABB means lines 1-2 rhyme and lines 3-4 rhyme.
The speaker of a poem is the voice saying the words (often 'I' or 'me').
Poets use repetition (repeating words like 'Let me be') to make an idea stronger and give the poem a rhythm.
The poem's second stanza (also original): 'Let me be kind when you are wrong, / And help you up and make you strong; / For friendship isn't gold or gift — / It's a hand held out, a heart to lift.'

ex.q: Read this original stanza: Let me be the friend who listens well, / Who keeps the secrets you choose to tell, / Who shares an umbrella when rain falls down, / And gently turns away your frown. What is its rhyme scheme?
st: Last words: well, tell, down, frown.
'well' and 'tell' rhyme → A A.
'down' and 'frown' rhyme → B B.
ex.a: AABB

topics.rl: Friendship bands on Friendship Day, birthday cards and school farewell speeches often use short rhyming poems like this.

topics.h: Add three little letters to 'kind' and you get 'kindness' — a word that can change someone's whole day!
p: Kindness means being friendly, caring and helpful to others, without expecting anything back.
The suffix -ness turns adjectives into nouns: kind → kindness, happy → happiness, sad → sadness.
The suffix -ful means 'full of': care → careful, help → helpful, thank → thankful. The suffix -less means 'without': care → careless, help → helpless.
The prefix un- means 'not': kind → unkind, fair → unfair, friendly → unfriendly.
Small acts of kindness: sharing, listening, including a new student, saying 'thank you' and 'sorry'.

ex.q: Think it through: Make two new words from 'help', one meaning 'full of help' and one meaning 'without help'.
st: -ful means 'full of' → helpful.
-less means 'without' → helpless.
ex.a: helpful and helpless

topics.rl: Helping a younger child find their classroom, or inviting a new student to sit with you at lunch, are everyday acts of kindness.

topics.h: Imagine saying 'Tara said Tara will lend Tara's book to Tara's friend.' Pronouns save us from that tongue-twister!
p: A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun: Tara → she, the book → it, Tara and I → we.
Subject pronouns do the action: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Object pronouns receive the action: me, you, him, her, it, us, them.
Possessive pronouns show ownership and stand alone: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs ('This pencil is mine').
Reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves ('She taught herself to paint').
Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: 'yours', not 'your's'; 'its' (belonging to it) is different from 'it's' (it is).

ex.q: Think it through: Replace the repeated nouns: 'Arjun lost Arjun's bag, so Priya helped Arjun find the bag.'
st: 'Arjun's' → his.
Second 'Arjun' (object of 'helped') → him.
'the bag' → it.
ex.a: Arjun lost his bag, so Priya helped him find it.

topics.rl: Whenever you chat with friends — 'Is this yours?' 'No, it's mine!' — you're using pronouns.

topics.t: A story told by a chair
topics.h: What if the chair you're sitting on could talk? What stories would it tell about you?
p: 'The Chair' is a story that centres on an ordinary chair and the feelings and imagination around it.
When a non-living thing is given human feelings or actions, it is called personification ('the chair felt young again').
A story told by 'I' is in the first person. The narrator here is the chair itself.
The setting is where and when a story happens; the characters are the people, animals or things in it.
Readers can infer (work out) feelings from clues, even when the feeling is not named.

ex.q: Read: I am an old wooden chair on Nani's verandah. For forty years I have held tired visitors, giggling grandchildren and one very fat cat. My legs creak now, and yesterday someone said, "Let's throw it away." But little Chintu painted my arms blue and said, "You're my throne!" I felt young again. How does the chair feel at the start and at the end?
st: 'My legs creak now' and 'Let's throw it away' suggest the chair feels old and unwanted.
Chintu paints it and calls it his throne.
'I felt young again' shows it now feels happy and loved.
ex.a: At first it feels old and unwanted; at the end it feels young, happy and loved.

topics.rl: Many families keep an old chair, almirah or trunk for years — each one 'remembers' family stories!

topics.h: A blanket can be a tent, a broom can be a horse, and a chair can be a throne — all you need is imagination!
p: Imagination is the power to form pictures and ideas in your mind of things that are not really present.
Every story has characters (who), a setting (where and when) and a plot (what happens, with a problem and an ending).
Writers often start with a 'What if...?' question: What if my school bag could fly?
Word family: imagine (verb), imagination (noun), imaginative (adjective), imaginary (adjective: not real).
'Imaginative' describes a creative person or idea; 'imaginary' describes something that exists only in the mind.

ex.q: Think it through: Ananya writes: 'What if the old chair could walk at night?' Name the parts she needs to build a story.
st: Character: the old chair (and maybe the family).
Setting: the house, at night.
Plot: a problem (the chair wants to explore) and an ending (it returns before morning).
ex.a: She needs characters, a setting and a plot with a problem and an ending.

topics.rl: Cardboard-box rockets, rangoli designs and the games you invent with friends all come from imagination.

topics.h: Empathy is like trying on someone else's shoes — even a chair's! — to feel what they feel.
p: Empathy means understanding and sharing the feelings of another person (or imagining how a thing or animal might feel).
Sympathy is feeling sorry for someone; empathy goes further — you imagine yourself in their place.
Feeling words help us show empathy: lonely, hurt, proud, grateful, nervous, relieved.
Conjunctions are joining words: and (adds), but (contrasts), or (gives a choice), so (shows result), because (gives a reason).
Example: 'The chair felt sad because someone wanted to throw it away, but Chintu loved it.'

ex.q: Think it through: Join with the right conjunction: 'Meena's friend was crying. Meena sat beside her and listened.'
st: The second sentence is the result of the first.
'So' shows a result.
Join them.
ex.a: Meena's friend was crying, so Meena sat beside her and listened.

topics.rl: When a classmate loses a match or a pet, saying 'I can imagine how hard that is' shows empathy.

topics.t: The neem tree and its uses
topics.h: Why would anyone brush their teeth with a twig? Meet the neem tree — India's bitter but brilliant friend!
p: 'Neem Baba' is a lesson about the neem tree and the many ways it helps people.
The neem tree (scientific name Azadirachta indica) is native to the Indian subcontinent and grows well in hot, dry places.
Its leaves taste bitter. Traditionally, neem twigs (called 'datun') have been used to clean teeth.
People traditionally keep dried neem leaves with stored grains and woollen clothes to keep insects away. Oil from neem seeds is used in some soaps and natural insect repellents.
A big neem tree gives cool shade, and its small white flowers smell sweet.

ex.q: Read: Outside our school stands a huge neem tree. Its bitter leaves rustle in the breeze, and its thick branches give cool shade in May. Grandpa still cleans his teeth with a neem twig. Every year Ma puts dried neem leaves in the rice tin to keep insects away. The children call the tree 'Neem Baba' because it seems wise, old and kind. Give two uses of the neem tree from the passage.
st: Grandpa cleans his teeth with a neem twig → use 1.
Ma keeps dried neem leaves in the rice tin to keep insects away → use 2.
Its branches give cool shade → use 3.
ex.a: Any two: cleaning teeth with a twig, keeping insects away from rice, giving cool shade.

topics.rl: You may see neem trees along roads and in school compounds, and neem in soaps and toothpastes on shop shelves.

topics.h: One tree can give shade to a whole playground for a hundred years. What can one child give back?
p: Conservation means protecting and carefully using nature — trees, water, animals and soil — so that it lasts for the future.
We can help by planting trees, saving water, not wasting paper and following the 3 Rs: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle.
Van Mahotsav, a tree-planting festival, is celebrated in India in the first week of July. World Environment Day is on 5 June.
In the Chipko movement of the 1970s, villagers in the Himalayan hills hugged trees to stop them from being cut down. ('Chipko' means 'to stick' or 'hug'.)
Compound words join two words to make one: rain + water = rainwater; sun + light = sunlight; wild + life = wildlife.

ex.q: Think it through: Sort these actions into Reduce, Reuse or Recycle: carrying a cloth bag instead of taking a new plastic one; using an old jam jar as a pencil holder; sending old newspapers to be made into new paper.
st: Not taking a new plastic bag means using less → Reduce.
Using the jar again for a new job → Reuse.
Turning old paper into new paper → Recycle.
ex.a: Cloth bag → Reduce; jam jar pencil holder → Reuse; newspapers to make new paper → Recycle.

topics.rl: Turning off the tap while brushing, carrying a steel water bottle and planting a sapling on your birthday are everyday conservation.

topics.h: Where is the bird? In the tree, on the branch, among the leaves — prepositions are word maps!
p: A preposition shows the relation of a noun or pronoun to another word — often place, time or direction.
Place: in (inside), on (touching the surface), under (below), beside (next to), between (two things), among (more than two).
Time: at for exact times (at 7 o'clock), on for days and dates (on Monday, on 5 June), in for months, years and seasons (in July, in 2024, in summer).
Use 'since' for a starting point (since 2015) and 'for' for a length of time (for ten years).
Direction: into, out of, across, through, towards ('The squirrel ran up the trunk').

ex.q: Think it through: Fill in: 'The children sat ___ the shade of the neem tree ___ 4 o'clock ___ Sunday.'
st: 'Shade' is an area we are inside → in.
An exact clock time → at.
A day of the week → on.
ex.a: in, at, on

topics.rl: Giving directions — 'The shop is beside the temple, across the road' — uses prepositions all the time.

topics.t: The world through a bird's eyes
topics.h: Ever wondered what your school looks like to a kite flying overhead? Let's borrow a bird's wings!
p: 'What a Bird Thought' is a poem about how a bird sees and thinks about the world around it.
In a poem, the speaker may be an animal or a thing, not a person. Here the speaker is a bird.
A 'bird's-eye view' means a view from high above, where big things look small.
Poets use images (word pictures) so we can see what the speaker sees.
To understand a poem, read it twice, picture each line, and ask: Who is speaking? What do they see? How do they feel?

ex.q: Read this original poem: From high above, the town looks small, / The cars are scattered painted toys; / The river is a silver thread, / The bus, a beetle, makes no noise. / I wonder if the people know / How tiny all their worries seem / When seen from up among the clouds, / Where every road is like a dream. Who is the speaker and what do they notice?
st: 'From high above' and 'among the clouds' show the speaker is flying — a bird.
The bird sees cars like toys, the river like a thread, the bus like a beetle.
It also wonders whether people know how small their worries look from above.
ex.a: A bird flying high; it notices that everything below looks tiny, and so do people's worries.

topics.rl: Photos taken by drones or from aeroplane windows give us a bird's-eye view of fields, rivers and cities.

topics.t: Seeing from another point of view
topics.h: To an ant, a puddle is an ocean. To you, it's just a puddle. Who is right? Both!
p: Perspective (point of view) is the way someone sees or thinks about something. It depends on where they are and what they know.
The same event can look different to different people: rain is a joy for a farmer but a problem for a cricket match.
First-person writing uses 'I', 'me', 'we' (the narrator is in the story). Third-person writing uses 'he', 'she', 'they' (the narrator is outside the story).
Changing the point of view can change how a story feels. Imagine your school day told by your school bag!
Seeing other perspectives helps us understand people better and avoid quick judgements.

ex.q: Think it through: Rewrite in the first person, as if the bird is speaking: 'The bird looked down and saw the town.'
st: The narrator becomes the bird itself.
Replace 'The bird' with 'I'.
Keep the rest of the sentence.
ex.a: I looked down and saw the town.

topics.rl: In a cricket match, a 'no-ball' may look different to the batter, the bowler and the umpire — that's why we have replays!

topics.h: 'The bus is like a beetle' and 'The bus is a beetle' — one little word makes all the difference!
p: A simile compares two different things using 'like' or 'as': 'The cars look like toys', 'as light as a feather'.
A metaphor compares by saying one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as': 'The river is a silver thread.'
Both help readers picture something clearly and in a fresh way.
Common similes: as busy as a bee, as brave as a lion, as cool as a cucumber, as white as snow, as slow as a snail.
Tip: look for 'like' or 'as ... as' to spot a simile; if one thing is simply called another, it is a metaphor.

ex.q: Think it through: Is this a simile or a metaphor? 'Grandma's lap is a soft pillow.'
st: Look for 'like' or 'as' — there isn't one.
It says the lap IS a pillow.
So it is a metaphor.
ex.a: A metaphor.

topics.rl: Cricket commentators love them: 'He's a wall at the crease!' (metaphor) or 'The ball flew like a rocket!' (simile).

topics.h: Your kitchen masala box is a treasure chest — full of colours, smells and centuries of wisdom!
p: 'Spices that Heal Us' is an informative lesson about common Indian spices and how they have traditionally been used for good health.
Turmeric (haldi) is the bright yellow powder made from the underground stem of the turmeric plant. Haldi milk is a popular home drink for colds.
Ginger (adrak) is also an underground stem. Ginger tea is a common home remedy for a sore throat.
Cloves (laung) are dried flower buds, cinnamon (dalchini) is tree bark, and black pepper (kali mirch) is a dried fruit of a climbing vine.
Home remedies can soothe small troubles, but a doctor must treat real illnesses. Never eat spices in large amounts as 'medicine'.

ex.q: Read: When Aman caught a cold, Nani made him a cup of warm milk with a pinch of haldi. The next day she brewed ginger tea with tulsi leaves. "These spices have been used in Indian kitchens for centuries," she said. "They add flavour, and many people use them for small troubles like a sore throat. But for a real illness, we always visit the doctor." Name the two drinks Nani made, and what she says about real illness.
st: Day 1: warm milk with haldi.
Day 2: ginger tea with tulsi leaves.
Her last line: for a real illness, we always visit the doctor.
ex.a: Haldi milk and ginger-tulsi tea; for a real illness, the family visits the doctor.

topics.rl: Haldi in dal, jeera in rice, elaichi in kheer and ginger in chai — spices are in almost every Indian meal.

topics.h: Your grandparents know things no textbook taught them — like which leaf soothes a cough. That's traditional knowledge!
p: Traditional knowledge is wisdom that people learn by experience and pass down from one generation to the next, often by word of mouth.
In India, knowledge about spices, plants, farming and cooking has been shared within families for centuries.

Spices come from different plant parts: seeds (jeera, ajwain, methi), bark (cinnamon), flower buds (cloves), underground stems (ginger, turmeric), fruits (black pepper), and flower parts (saffron comes from the thread-like parts of a crocus flower).
Kerala is famous for growing spices like black pepper and cardamom; Kashmir is famous for saffron (kesar).
Useful words: generation, heritage, remedy, ancestor, ingredient.

ex.q: Think it through: Mira's great-grandmother taught her grandmother, who taught her mother, who taught Mira how to make jeera water. What kind of knowledge is this, and how was it passed on?
st: It moved from grandparent to parent to child.
It was learnt by practice in the kitchen, not from a textbook.
Knowledge passed down through generations is traditional knowledge.
ex.a: Traditional knowledge, passed down from one generation to the next.

topics.rl: Grandma's recipe for achaar, the way farmers read the clouds, and Mehendi patterns are all traditional knowledge.

topics.t: A, an, the and much or many
topics.h: Is it 'a onion' or 'an onion'? 'Much cloves' or 'many cloves'? Let's spice up our grammar!
p: Use 'a' before a consonant SOUND (a clove, a university) and 'an' before a vowel SOUND (an onion, an hour). Listen to the sound, not the letter.
Use 'the' for something specific or already mentioned: 'I bought a lemon. The lemon was juicy.'
Countable nouns can be counted: one clove, two cloves. Uncountable nouns cannot: salt, water, milk, rice, advice.
Use 'many' and 'a few' with countable nouns; 'much' and 'a little' with uncountable nouns.
We count uncountable nouns using measure words: a pinch of salt, a cup of milk, a spoonful of honey.

ex.q: Think it through: Fill in: 'Nani added ___ pinch of salt and ___ few cloves, but not ___ ginger.' (choose from a / an / much / many)
st: 'pinch' starts with a consonant sound → a pinch.
'cloves' are countable → a few cloves.
'ginger' here is uncountable → much ginger.
ex.a: a pinch, a few cloves, not much ginger

topics.rl: Recipes are full of these: 'a cup of rice', 'an onion', 'a little oil', 'many curry leaves'.

topics.h: Can you lose a match and still be the hero of the day? This story says yes!
p: 'Change of Heart' is a sports story about how a person's feelings and choices can change.
A 'change of heart' is an idiom meaning a change in one's opinion or feelings, usually towards something kinder.
Sports stories have a goal (winning), a conflict (a tough opponent or a hard choice) and a turning point.
Kabaddi is a team sport from India in which a 'raider' enters the other half and tries to tag opponents while saying 'kabaddi, kabaddi'.
When reading, note how a character's thoughts at the start differ from their actions at the end.

ex.q: Read: Sana wanted to win the kabaddi final at any cost. Late in the match, the rival captain, Divya, slipped and twisted her ankle. "Keep going! Now we'll win easily!" shouted Sana's teammates. But when Sana saw Divya wince in pain, she had a change of heart. She stopped, helped Divya up and called for the first-aid kit. Sana's team lost by two points, yet the whole crowd clapped for her. What was Sana's change of heart?
st: At the start she wanted to win 'at any cost'.
When Divya got hurt, her teammates wanted to keep playing.
Sana saw Divya's pain and stopped to help her.
She chose kindness over winning.
ex.a: She stopped caring only about winning and helped her injured rival instead.

topics.rl: Some real athletes have stopped to help a fallen rival in races — and crowds remember those moments longer than the results.

topics.h: The scoreboard shows who won the game. Sportsmanship shows who won respect.
p: Sportsmanship means playing fairly, following the rules, respecting opponents and accepting results gracefully.
A 'good sport' wins without boasting and loses without sulking.
Useful words: fair play, opponent (the person you play against), teammate, referee/umpire, gracious, honour.
Opposites: win ↔ lose, victory ↔ defeat, fair ↔ unfair, teammate ↔ opponent.
Shaking hands after a match, cheering good play by the other side and accepting the umpire's decision are signs of sportsmanship.

ex.q: Think it through: In a cricket match, Kiran knows the ball touched his bat before the catch, but the umpire did not see it. He walks off the field anyway. What does this show?
st: Kiran could have stayed because the umpire missed it.
He chose honesty over his own score.
Being honest and fair in sport is sportsmanship.
ex.a: It shows honesty and good sportsmanship.

topics.rl: At the end of every match, players shake hands — a small habit that shows respect, whoever wins.

topics.t: Adverbs: how, when, where, how often
topics.h: Sana ran FAST, helped KINDLY and played FAIRLY. Those capital words are adverbs — let's meet them!
p: An adverb tells us more about a verb (and sometimes an adjective or another adverb).
Adverbs of manner tell how: quickly, bravely, kindly, carefully. Many are made by adding -ly to adjectives (quick → quickly).
Adverbs of time tell when (now, soon, yesterday); of place tell where (here, there, outside); of frequency tell how often (always, often, sometimes, never).
Some adverbs don't end in -ly: fast, hard, well, late. 'Good' is an adjective; its adverb is 'well' (She plays well).
Careful: 'hardly' means 'almost not'. 'He worked hard' is very different from 'He hardly worked'!

ex.q: Think it through: Find the adverbs and what they tell us: 'Yesterday, Sana played bravely outside.'
st: 'Yesterday' tells when → time.
'bravely' tells how she played → manner.
'outside' tells where → place.
ex.a: yesterday (time), bravely (manner), outside (place)

topics.rl: Sports commentary is full of adverbs: 'He bowled quickly', 'She always smiles', 'They played well today.'

topics.h: Who is the real winner — the one who comes first, or the one who never gives up?
p: 'The Winner' is a poem about what it really means to win: effort, courage and not giving up.
A poem can make us rethink a word. Here, 'winning' means doing your best, not only coming first.
Couplets are pairs of lines that rhyme. A poem made of rhyming couplets has the rhyme scheme AABBCC...
Poets use images like 'a fire inside' to show strong feelings such as determination.
Read a poem aloud to feel its rhythm — the beat of strong and soft sounds.

ex.q: Read this original poem: I tripped on the track and I heard the loud cheer / For the runners ahead as the finish drew near; / My knees were all scraped and my laces untied, / But I stood up again with a fire inside. / I came in last, but I crossed the line — / And the medal of trying is shining and mine. Why does the speaker feel like a winner?
st: The speaker tripped, got hurt and came in last.
But they stood up again 'with a fire inside' and crossed the line.
They call their effort 'the medal of trying'.
ex.a: Because they did not give up — they got up and finished the race, and that effort is their 'medal'.

topics.rl: School sports days give medals to the top three, but everyone who finishes the race has shown courage.

topics.h: A spider fails seven times to climb its thread and climbs on the eighth. That spider knows a big word: perseverance!
p: Perseverance means continuing to try even when something is difficult or takes a long time.
Word family: persevere (verb), perseverance (noun), persevering (adjective). Similar words: determination, persistence, grit.
The opposite of persevering is giving up or quitting.
Proverbs about perseverance: 'Practice makes perfect', 'Slow and steady wins the race', 'Where there's a will, there's a way'.
Perseverance works best with good habits: setting small goals, practising daily and learning from mistakes.

ex.q: Think it through: Neha cannot ride her bicycle and falls three times. She asks her brother to hold the seat and practises every evening for a week. Finally she rides alone. Which proverb fits?
st: Neha keeps trying after falling.
She practises every day.
Her practice leads to success.
ex.a: 'Practice makes perfect' (or 'Where there's a will, there's a way').

topics.rl: Learning to swim, playing a musical instrument or solving tough maths sums all need perseverance.

topics.h: 'I CAN win', 'I MUST practise', 'I SHOULD rest' — little helping verbs carry big meanings!
p: Modal verbs are helping verbs that add meaning to the main verb: can, could, may, might, must, should, will, would.
Can = ability ('I can run fast') or asking informally ('Can I go out?'). Could = past ability ('I could swim at six').
May = polite permission ('May I come in?') or possibility ('It may rain').
Must = something necessary or a strong duty ('You must wear a helmet'). Should = advice ('You should drink water').
After a modal, use the base verb with no 's', 'ed' or 'to': 'She can sing', not 'She can sings' or 'She can to sing'.

ex.q: Think it through: Choose the best modal: 'Players ___ follow the rules of the game.' (can / must / may)
st: Following rules is a duty, not just an ability or a possibility.
A strong duty is shown by 'must'.
ex.a: must

topics.rl: Rules and signs use modals: 'You must wear a seat belt', 'Visitors may take photos', 'You should wash your hands.'

topics.h: What can make you as steady as a mountain and as calm as a still lake — without any gadgets? Yoga!
p: 'Yoga — A Way of Life' is an informative lesson about yoga and how it helps the body and mind.
The word 'yoga' comes from the Sanskrit root 'yuj', which means 'to join' or 'to unite' — joining body, breath and mind.
Yoga includes asanas (postures), pranayama (breathing exercises) and meditation (quietly focusing the mind).
Benefits: better flexibility, strength and balance, a calmer mind and better concentration.
International Day of Yoga is celebrated every year on 21 June. The United Nations declared it in 2014, and it was first celebrated in 2015.

ex.q: Read: Every morning, Kavya unrolls her mat on the terrace. She begins with slow, deep breaths. Then she stands tall like a mountain and stretches like a tree. "Yoga makes my body flexible and my mind calm," she says. Since she started, she finds it easier to concentrate on her studies, and she rarely feels stiff after long hours at her desk. List two benefits of yoga that Kavya mentions or experiences.
st: Kavya says yoga makes her body flexible.
She says it makes her mind calm.
She finds it easier to concentrate and rarely feels stiff.
ex.a: Any two: a flexible body, a calm mind, better concentration, less stiffness.

topics.rl: Many schools hold a yoga session on 21 June, and lots of families begin their day with a few asanas and pranayama.

topics.h: Your body is like a phone: it needs charging (sleep), good fuel (food) and the right apps (exercise)!
p: A healthy lifestyle includes a balanced diet, regular exercise, enough sleep, cleanliness and a calm mind.
A balanced diet has the right amounts of different foods: grains, pulses, vegetables, fruits, milk products and water.
Instructions (like yoga steps) are written as imperative sentences that start with a verb: 'Stand straight.' 'Breathe in slowly.'
Sequence words make instructions clear: first, next, then, after that, finally.
Safety in yoga: practise on a mat with an empty or light stomach, learn from a trained teacher, and never force a pose that hurts.

ex.q: Think it through: Turn this into instructions for the tree pose (Vrikshasana): stand straight; raise one foot to the inside of the other leg; join palms; hold; come back.
st: Begin each step with a verb.
Add sequence words.
Keep it simple and safe.
ex.a: First, stand straight. Next, place your right foot on the inside of your left leg (not on the knee). Then join your palms. Hold and breathe. Finally, lower your foot and repeat on the other side.

topics.rl: Recipes, game rules and science-activity steps are all written as imperative instructions with sequence words.

topics.h: Some sentences tell, some ask, some order and some shout with joy. Can you tell which is which?
p: A declarative (assertive) sentence makes a statement and ends with a full stop: 'Yoga keeps us fit.'
An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark: 'Do you practise yoga?'
An imperative sentence gives a command, request or instruction: 'Stand straight.' 'Please close the door.'
An exclamatory sentence shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark: 'What a lovely morning!'
In imperative sentences the subject 'you' is usually understood, not written.

ex.q: Think it through: Identify each: (a) Breathe in deeply. (b) How calm I feel! (c) Is yoga easy? (d) Kavya does yoga daily.
st: (a) gives an instruction → imperative.
(b) shows strong feeling → exclamatory.
(c) asks → interrogative.
(d) states a fact → declarative.
ex.a: (a) imperative, (b) exclamatory, (c) interrogative, (d) declarative

topics.rl: Notice them in daily life: 'Close the door.' (imperative), 'Where's my bag?' (interrogative), 'What a goal!' (exclamatory).

topics.h: Travel a few hundred kilometres in India and the language, food and clothes may all change — yet everyone is Indian!
p: 'Hamara Bharat — Incredible India!' is a lesson about the amazing variety of India's land, people and ways of life.
Diversity means variety — many different kinds. India has diversity in languages, food, clothes, festivals, music, dance and landscape.
India has 28 states and 8 union territories. The Constitution lists 22 languages in its Eighth Schedule, and many more are spoken.
Landscapes range from the snowy Himalayas to the Thar Desert in Rajasthan, the mangrove forests of the Sundarbans and long coastlines.
'Unity in diversity' means that, despite our differences, we are united as one nation.

ex.q: Read: In Asha's class, Arjun's family is from Punjab, Lalitha's from Tamil Nadu, Joseph's from Kerala and Rinku's from Assam. At lunch, the tiffins open: makki di roti, curd rice, appam and pitha. Arjun says 'Sat Sri Akal', Lalitha says 'Vanakkam' and Rinku says 'Nomoskar'. Different foods, different greetings — one happy class. What does this passage show about India?
st: Four classmates come from four different states.
They eat different foods and use different greetings.
Yet they form 'one happy class'.
ex.a: It shows unity in diversity: different foods and languages, but one united class (like one united India).

topics.rl: Look around your own class: different home languages, festivals and tiffins — that's India's diversity in one room!

topics.h: From Garba nights to Bihu dances and Onam feasts, India celebrates almost every week of the year!
p: Culture is the way of life of a group of people: their language, food, clothes, music, dance, art and festivals.
Traditions are customs and beliefs passed down from one generation to the next.

Classical dances of India include Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathakali (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha) and Manipuri (Manipur). Folk dances include Bhangra (Punjab), Garba (Gujarat), Bihu (Assam) and Ghoomar (Rajasthan).
Harvest festivals are celebrated in different ways: Pongal (Tamil Nadu), Onam (Kerala), Bihu (Assam), Baisakhi (Punjab).
People of all communities celebrate festivals like Diwali, Eid, Christmas, Guru Nanak Jayanti and Buddha Purnima, and neighbours often join in each other's celebrations.

ex.q: Think it through: Ravi's family in Kerala celebrates a harvest festival with a big feast on banana leaves and a flower carpet (pookalam). Which festival is it?
st: The state is Kerala.
A harvest festival with a feast (sadya) and a flower carpet (pookalam).
That is Onam.
ex.a: Onam

topics.rl: School annual days often have a 'unity in diversity' dance show with Bhangra, Garba, Bihu and Bharatanatyam on one stage.

topics.h: 'India have many languages' or 'India has many languages'? Let's make subjects and verbs agree!
p: The verb must agree with its subject in number: a singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb.
In the simple present, singular subjects (he, she, it, one name) take verbs with -s/-es: 'Ravi dances.' Plural subjects don't: 'They dance.'
is/was/has go with singular subjects; are/were/have go with plural subjects. 'I am', 'you are' are special.
Two subjects joined by 'and' are plural: 'Asha and Ravi are friends.'
Words like each, every, everyone, everybody take a singular verb: 'Everyone loves Diwali sweets.' 'One of the states is Goa.'

ex.q: Think it through: Correct the sentence: 'Each of the students have a different tiffin.'
st: The real subject is 'Each' (one at a time), not 'students'.
'Each' is singular.
Singular subject → 'has'.
ex.a: Each of the students has a different tiffin.

topics.rl: Writing a postcard home — 'The beaches are lovely and the food is delicious' — needs subject-verb agreement.

topics.h: Whoosh! Swoosh! Can you hear a poem? Some poems are made to be heard as much as read!
p: 'The Kites' is a poem about the joy and colour of kites flying in the sky.
Onomatopoeia: words that sound like what they describe (whoosh, swoosh, flutter, snap).
Alliteration: the same first sound repeated in words close together ('bright, breezy day').
Personification: kites 'go dancing', as if they were people. A metaphor: 'The sky is a garden.'
Rhyme and rhythm make a poem feel like the swaying, rising and dipping of a kite.

ex.q: Read this original poem: Up on the roof on a bright, breezy day, / Red kites and green kites go dancing away; / The string in my hand hums whoosh, whoosh, whoosh, / As up goes my kite with a swoop and a swoosh. / "Kai po che!" shouts my cousin with glee — / The sky is a garden as far as I see. Find one example each of onomatopoeia, alliteration and metaphor.
st: Sound words: 'whoosh' and 'swoosh' → onomatopoeia.
'bright, breezy' repeat the 'b' sound → alliteration.
'The sky is a garden' calls the sky a garden without 'like' → metaphor.
ex.a: Onomatopoeia: whoosh/swoosh; alliteration: bright, breezy; metaphor: the sky is a garden.

topics.rl: On kite-flying days, rooftops fill with shouts, whistles and the whirr of the spool — a real-life sound poem!

topics.h: In January, the skies over many Indian cities fill with thousands of kites. Which festival is it?
p: Makar Sankranti, in January, marks the sun's movement into Makara (Capricorn). It is a harvest-time festival celebrated across India by different names.
In Gujarat it is called Uttarayan, and people fly kites from rooftops all day. Ahmedabad hosts a famous International Kite Festival.
In Tamil Nadu the same season brings Pongal; in Punjab, Lohri is celebrated the night before Makar Sankranti; in Assam, it is Magh (Bhogali) Bihu.
Kites are also flown on Independence Day (15 August) in Delhi and other places.
Kite safety: never use glass-coated or nylon string (manja) — it hurts birds and people; stay away from electric wires; fly only from safe places with an adult nearby.

ex.q: Think it through: Rehan wants to fly kites on Uttarayan with glass-coated manja from the edge of the roof near an electric wire. What three things should he change?
st: Glass-coated manja can cut birds and people → use plain cotton thread.
The edge of the roof is dangerous → stay in a safe, railed area with an adult.
Electric wires are dangerous → fly far away from them.
ex.a: Use plain cotton thread, stay in a safe place with an adult, and keep away from electric wires.

topics.rl: Bird hospitals and volunteers in Gujarat work extra hard during Uttarayan to help birds hurt by sharp manja — safe string saves lives.

topics.h: Look up! The kites ARE FLYING, my cousin IS SHOUTING and I AM HOLDING the string — all right now!
p: The present continuous tense describes an action happening now: am/is/are + verb + -ing.
I am flying; he/she/it is flying; we/you/they are flying.
Spelling: most verbs add -ing (fly → flying); drop silent -e (make → making); double the last letter after a short vowel (run → running); -ie becomes -y (tie → tying).
Negative: am/is/are + not + -ing ('She is not flying a kite'). Question: Am/Is/Are + subject + -ing? ('Are you flying a kite?')
Verbs of thinking and feeling such as know, like, want, believe are usually NOT used in the continuous: say 'I know', not 'I am knowing'.

ex.q: Think it through: Change to the present continuous: 'My cousin cuts the kite and shouts.'
st: Subject 'my cousin' is singular → is.
cut → cutting (double the t).
shout → shouting.
Join with 'and'.
ex.a: My cousin is cutting the kite and shouting.

topics.rl: Live cricket commentary is full of it: 'He is running in, he is bowling... and the batter is hitting it for six!'

topics.ch: Ila Sachani: Embroidering Dreams with her Feet
topics.h: Some heroes don't wear capes. They hold a needle, a sitar or a paintbrush — and they never give up.
p: 'Ila Sachani: Embroidering Dreams with her Feet' tells the real-life story of Ila Sachani, who creates beautiful embroidery using her feet.
A biography is the true story of a person's life written by someone else, in the third person (he, she, they).
An autobiography is a person's life story written by that person, in the first person (I, me, my).
Life stories are usually told in time order (chronological order) and in the past tense.
Embroidery words: needle, thread, stitch, fabric (cloth), pattern, design.

ex.q: Read: (An original life story.) Kiran was born in a small town and lost her sight when she was seven. At first she felt afraid of the dark world around her. Then a teacher taught her Braille, and books opened up again. She practised the sitar for hours every day. At twenty-five, she gave her first concert, and today she teaches music to children who are blind. Put the main events of Kiran's life in order and say what makes her story inspiring.
st: Lost her sight at seven and felt afraid.
Learnt Braille and could read again.
Practised the sitar every day.
Gave her first concert at twenty-five.
Now teaches music to blind children.
ex.a: Events in order: loses sight → learns Braille → practises sitar → first concert → teaches others. It is inspiring because she overcame fear through hard work and now helps others.

topics.rl: School libraries often have biographies of scientists, athletes and artists — real people whose lives inspire us.

topics.ch: Ila Sachani: Embroidering Dreams with her Feet
topics.h: What matters more — what you cannot do, or what you choose to do with what you can?
p: A disability is a condition that makes some activities, like seeing, hearing, walking or using one's hands, harder in the usual way. People with disabilities find their own ways and tools to do things.
Use respectful words: 'a person with a disability', 'a wheelchair user', 'a person who is blind'. In India, the word 'Divyang' is also used officially.
Determination means a firm decision to achieve something, however hard it is.
Accessibility means making places and things usable by everyone: ramps, lifts, Braille signs, audio books and Indian Sign Language.
Indian para-athletes such as Avani Lekhara (shooting) have won gold medals at the Paralympic Games.

ex.q: Think it through: A new classmate uses a wheelchair, and the class library is up a flight of stairs. What could the class do, and which values does this show?
st: The problem is access, not the classmate.
Ask the school to use a ramp, a lift or a ground-floor library corner.
Ask the classmate what would help — and include them.
ex.a: Request a ramp or move books to the ground floor and include the classmate; this shows empathy, respect and fairness.

topics.rl: Ramps at railway stations, Braille on lift buttons and sign-language windows on TV news are accessibility in action.

topics.ch: Ila Sachani: Embroidering Dreams with her Feet
topics.h: She can SEW a flower, a farmer can SOW a seed, SO what's the difference? Spelling!
p: Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings and spellings.
sew (to stitch with needle and thread), sow (to plant seeds), so (therefore / very).
there (a place), their (belonging to them), they're (they are).
to (towards), too (also / very much), two (the number 2).
More pairs: hear/here, write/right, knew/new, piece/peace, threw/through, sea/see.

ex.q: Think it through: Choose the right words: 'Ila can (sew/sow) a (piece/peace) of cloth with her feet, and (their/there) are many who admire her.'
st: Stitching cloth → sew.
A part of something → piece.
'There are' (introducing something) → there.
ex.a: sew, piece, there

topics.rl: Spell-check can't always help: 'I red the book' is spelt correctly but wrong! Knowing homophones makes your writing clear.

topics.h: Some names are carved in stone so that a whole nation never forgets them.
p: 'National War Memorial' is a lesson about the memorial built to honour India's soldiers.
The National War Memorial is in New Delhi, near India Gate. It was inaugurated in 2019 to honour soldiers who gave their lives defending India since Independence.

It is built as four circles (chakras): Amar Chakra (circle of immortality, with an eternal flame), Veerta Chakra (circle of bravery), Tyag Chakra (circle of sacrifice, with soldiers' names on granite walls) and Rakshak Chakra (circle of protection, a ring of trees).
The Param Vir Chakra is India's highest award for bravery during war.
Words of honour: memorial, tribute, sacrifice, salute, valour (great bravery), martyr.

ex.q: Read: Early one winter morning, our class visited the National War Memorial in New Delhi. A golden flame burned quietly at the centre. Around it, rings of granite walls carried thousands of names. We walked slowly and spoke in whispers. Our teacher said, "Each name belongs to a soldier who gave their life for our country." Nobody spoke for a long moment. Why did the children speak in whispers?
st: The place is a memorial for soldiers who died for India.
The teacher explains that each name is a soldier who gave their life.
Speaking softly shows respect for them.
ex.a: They spoke softly out of respect for the soldiers who gave their lives for the country.

topics.rl: On days like Republic Day and Independence Day, and at memorials across India, people lay wreaths and observe silence to honour soldiers.

topics.h: You don't need a uniform to serve India. A clean street, a kind act and an honest answer count too!
p: Patriotism means love for and pride in one's country, and a wish to work for its good.
Children can show patriotism by respecting the National Flag and National Anthem, keeping public places clean, following rules, saving water and electricity, and helping others.
The National Anthem, 'Jana Gana Mana', was written by Rabindranath Tagore. We stand still and silent when it is played.
The National Flag has three bands — saffron (strength and courage), white (peace and truth) and green (growth and fertility of the land) — with a navy-blue Ashoka Chakra of 24 spokes in the centre.
Word family: patriot (a person), patriotism (noun), patriotic (adjective).

ex.q: Think it through: After a cricket match, Rohan sees the stadium full of litter and paper flags lying on the ground. He picks up the paper flags respectfully and puts the litter in a bin. Is this patriotism?
st: He shows respect for the national flag.
He keeps a public place clean.
Both are ways of caring for the country.
ex.a: Yes — respecting the flag and keeping public places clean are everyday patriotism.

topics.rl: Taking part in a Swachhata (cleanliness) drive at school, or standing still for the anthem at the school assembly, are patriotic acts.

topics.h: Good descriptions are like teleporters — they carry the reader right into the place you saw!
p: Descriptive writing paints a picture with words so the reader can see, hear and feel a place, person or event.
Use the five senses: sight (golden flame), sound (soft whispers), touch (cold granite), smell (fresh grass), and sometimes taste.
Use exact adjectives and strong verbs: 'The flame flickered' is better than 'The fire was there'.
Organise details in an order: from near to far, from outside to inside, or from start to end of a visit.
A good paragraph has a topic sentence (main idea), supporting details, and a concluding sentence.

ex.q: Think it through: Improve this sentence: 'There was a fire and some walls with names.'
st: Use exact nouns and adjectives: a golden flame; tall granite walls.
Use a strong verb: flickered, rose.
Add a sense: the silence, the cold stone.
ex.a: A golden flame flickered at the centre, surrounded by tall granite walls carved with thousands of names.

topics.rl: Travel blogs, postcards home, and the school magazine's 'My Trip' page all use descriptive writing.

qa.q: Meera's story begins: "Meera wanted the best mangoes in the village. Her friend Kabir said, 'Just buy a magic powder!'" What did Meera want?
qa.a: The best mangoes in the village
qa.e: The first line says Meera wanted the best mangoes in the village.

qa.q: In Meera's story, Kabir said, "Just buy a magic powder and the tree will fruit overnight!" What is Kabir suggesting?
qa.e: A powder that works 'overnight' promises quick results with no effort, which is a shortcut.

qa.q: Meera "watered her little tree, pulled out weeds and added compost" every morning. This shows that Meera was:
qa.e: Doing the same useful work every day shows patience and hard work.

qa.q: In the story, Meera's tree gave mangoes "two summers later". What does this tell us?
qa.a: Good results can take a long time
qa.e: Two summers is a long time, so real results came slowly.

qa.q: What is the moral of Meera's mango story?
qa.a: Steady hard work brings real success
qa.e: Meera worked patiently and got sweet mangoes, so the story praises steady effort.

qa.q: Which word from Meera's story means 'very quickly, by the next morning'?
qa.e: Kabir promised the tree would fruit 'overnight', meaning by the next morning.

qa.q: Meera "shared them with everyone". What does this show about her?
qa.e: Sharing your mangoes with everyone is a generous act.

qa.q: Which is the best title for Meera's story?
qa.e: The story is about patient work leading to sweet mangoes, so 'Sweet Fruit of Patience' sums it up.

qa.q: Which word is a synonym of 'hard-working'?
qa.e: 'Diligent' means working carefully and steadily, just like 'hard-working'.

qa.q: What is the antonym of 'patient'?
qa.e: We add the prefix 'im-' to 'patient' to make 'impatient'.

qa.q: Choose the opposite of 'honest'.
qa.e: The opposite of 'honest' is formed with 'dis-': dishonest.

qa.q: Riya gives half of her laddoos to a friend who forgot his tiffin. Which value does she show?
qa.e: Giving away part of what you have to help someone is generosity.

qa.q: Which sentence shows patience?
qa.a: Sonu waited calmly for his turn on the swing.
qa.e: Waiting calmly for your turn is what patience means.

qa.q: Which word is the antonym of 'generous'?
qa.e: A generous person shares; a selfish person keeps everything for himself or herself.

qa.q: Which prefix makes the opposite of 'kind'?
qa.e: 'Kind' becomes 'unkind'. 'Re-' means 'again', not 'not'.

qa.q: A 'shortcut' in a story usually means:
qa.a: a quick, easy way that skips the real effort
qa.e: In stories about hard work, a shortcut is a way to get results quickly without doing the work.

qa.q: What is the simple past of 'carry'?
qa.e: For verbs ending in consonant + y, change y to i and add -ed: carry → carried.

qa.q: What is the simple past of 'buy'?
qa.e: 'Buy' is irregular: buy → bought. 'Brought' is the past of 'bring'.

qa.q: Which negative sentence in the past tense is correct?
qa.a: She did not take the shortcut.
qa.e: After 'did not' we use the base verb: did not take.

qa.q: Which verb is irregular?
qa.e: 'Go' becomes 'went'; the others just add -ed.

qa.q: Fill in: Last year, our class ___ a trip to the zoo.
qa.e: 'Last year' tells us the action is in the past, so we use 'made'.

qa.q: Change to a question: 'Kabir sold the powder.'
qa.e: Questions in the simple past use 'Did' + subject + base verb.

qa.q: What is the simple past of 'stop'?
qa.e: Short verbs ending in one vowel + one consonant double the last letter: stop → stopped.

qa.q: Which time word tells you to use the simple past?
qa.e: 'Yesterday' points to the past. 'Tomorrow' and 'next week' are future; 'every day' is a habit.

qa.q: What is a fable?
qa.a: A short story, often with talking animals, that teaches a moral
qa.e: Fables are short stories, usually with animal characters, that end with a lesson.

qa.q: 'The Raven and the Fox' is a fable 'in verse'. What does 'in verse' mean?
qa.e: Verse means poetry: lines with rhythm, often with rhyme.

qa.q: In the poem, which word rhymes with 'tight'?
qa.e: 'Tight' and 'delight' both end with the '-ight' sound.

qa.q: In the poem, the jackal said, "O bird so fair, your song must be a pure delight!" Why did he say this?
qa.a: To make the myna open her beak and drop the roti
qa.e: He wanted the roti, so he praised her to make her sing and drop it.

qa.q: In the poem, what happened when the myna sang out loud?
qa.a: The roti fell and the jackal grabbed it
qa.e: Opening her beak to sing made the roti fall, and the jackal ran off with it.

qa.q: What is the moral of the myna-and-jackal poem?
qa.a: Do not be fooled by sweet words of flattery
qa.e: The myna lost her food because she trusted the jackal's honeyed words.

qa.q: A group of lines in a poem is called a:
qa.e: Poems are divided into stanzas, just as prose is divided into paragraphs.

qa.q: Which ancient Indian collection is famous for animal fables?
qa.e: The Panchatantra is an ancient Indian collection of animal fables with morals.

qa.q: What is flattery?
qa.a: Too much praise, often not sincere, given to get something
qa.e: Flattery is exaggerated praise with a hidden purpose.

qa.q: Which sentence is honest praise?
qa.a: You batted well in today's match.
qa.e: It is true, fair and asks for nothing in return.

qa.q: A person who flatters others is called a:
qa.e: Adding -er to the verb 'flatter' gives the person who does it: flatterer.

qa.q: In the poem, the myna learns that "honeyed words can hide a plan that isn't right." 'Honeyed words' means:
qa.e: Honey is sweet, so 'honeyed words' are sweet-sounding words.

qa.q: 'Stop buttering me up!' What does 'buttering up' mean here?
qa.e: To butter someone up is an idiom meaning to flatter them to get something.

qa.q: What is the best thing to do when someone flatters you?
qa.a: Enjoy kind words but think about why they are said
qa.e: A wise person stays polite but thinks about the purpose behind the praise.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'sincere'?
qa.e: The opposite of 'sincere' is 'insincere', formed with the prefix 'in-'.

qa.q: Why do flatterers praise people too much?
qa.e: Flatterers use praise as a tool to get something, like the jackal and the roti.

qa.q: Which word is an adjective in: 'The hungry myna sat on a branch'?
qa.e: 'Hungry' describes the myna, so it is an adjective.

qa.q: What is the comparative degree of 'happy'?
qa.e: For adjectives ending in consonant + y, change y to i and add -er: happier.

qa.q: What is the superlative degree of 'good'?
qa.e: 'Good' is irregular: good, better, best.

qa.q: Which comparison of two people is correct?
qa.a: Rani is taller than her brother.
qa.e: Comparing two people needs the comparative form 'taller' with 'than'.

qa.q: Fill in: 'The Ganga is one of the ___ rivers in India.'
qa.e: 'One of the ...' is followed by a superlative: one of the longest rivers.

qa.q: What is the comparative of 'beautiful'?
qa.e: Long adjectives use 'more' for the comparative.

qa.q: What is the comparative of 'bad'?
qa.e: 'Bad' is irregular: bad, worse, worst.

qa.q: What is the superlative of 'big'?
qa.e: Short adjectives ending in one vowel + one consonant double the last letter: big → biggest.

qa.q: In the monkey story, what did the monkey snatch?
qa.e: The first line says the monkey snatched Dadaji's spectacles.

qa.q: In the story, "People shouted and waved, but the monkey only chattered." What does this show?
qa.a: Shouting did not solve the problem
qa.e: The monkey just chattered and did not return the spectacles, so shouting failed.

qa.q: How did Lata get the spectacles back?
qa.a: She held up a banana for the monkey
qa.e: The monkey dropped the spectacles to grab the banana Lata held up.

qa.q: Which word in the story is an example of onomatopoeia (a sound word)?
qa.e: 'Plop' imitates the sound of the spectacles dropping.

qa.q: What makes the monkey story humorous?
qa.a: A cheeky monkey and a funny swap of spectacles for a banana
qa.e: The silly monkey and the surprising swap make readers laugh.

qa.q: What is a folk tale?
qa.a: A traditional story passed on by people telling it
qa.e: Folk tales are old stories handed down by word of mouth.

qa.q: In the story, 'cheeky' monkey means the monkey was:
qa.e: A cheeky person or animal is playfully naughty and bold.

qa.q: How did the people feel at the end of the story?
qa.e: The story ends with 'Everyone laughed and clapped', which shows they were happy and amused.

qa.q: What does 'presence of mind' mean?
qa.a: Staying calm and thinking quickly in a sudden situation
qa.e: Presence of mind is about calm, quick thinking when something unexpected happens.

qa.q: In the monkey story, Lata 'stayed calm' and held up a banana. Which quality did she show?
qa.e: She stayed calm and found a quick, clever solution.

qa.q: What does 'quick-witted' mean?
qa.a: able to think fast and cleverly
qa.e: 'Wits' means the mind's cleverness, so quick-witted = fast, clever thinking.

qa.q: 'When the lights went out on stage, Arun kept a cool head and switched on his torch.' 'Kept a cool head' means he:
qa.e: To keep a cool head is an idiom for staying calm.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'calm'?
qa.e: 'Calm' means peaceful and relaxed; 'nervous' is its opposite.

qa.q: A 'resourceful' person is someone who:
qa.a: finds clever ways to solve problems
qa.e: Resourceful means good at finding solutions, especially in difficult situations.

qa.q: Your friend's kite string gets stuck on an electric wire. What shows presence of mind?
qa.a: Leave it and tell an adult; never pull it from the wire
qa.e: Electric wires are dangerous; the calm and safe choice is to leave it and inform an adult.

qa.q: 'Meena was at her wits' end when she lost her ticket.' This means Meena:
qa.a: did not know what to do
qa.e: Being at your wits' end means you are so worried you don't know what to do.

qa.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
qa.e: It has a comma after 'said', speech marks, a capital 'I' and the full stop inside the closing mark.

qa.q: Which mark ends a question?
qa.e: Questions end with a question mark (?).

qa.q: In 'Dadaji's spectacles', the apostrophe shows:
qa.a: that the spectacles belong to Dadaji
qa.e: Here 's shows possession: the spectacles belong to Dadaji.

qa.q: What is the short form of 'do not'?
qa.e: The apostrophe takes the place of the missing 'o': don't.

qa.q: Which word must always start with a capital letter?
qa.e: Jaipur is the name of a place, a proper noun, so it takes a capital letter.

qa.q: Which mark fits best? "Oh no___" cried Dadaji when the monkey took his glasses.
qa.e: 'Oh no' shows a strong feeling, so it takes an exclamation mark.

qa.q: Where do speech marks go?
qa.a: Around the exact words a person says
qa.e: Speech marks enclose only the words actually spoken.

qa.q: Which list is punctuated correctly?
qa.a: I packed a torch, a map and a water bottle.
qa.e: Commas separate items in a list, and 'and' joins the last two.

qa.q: In the story, Tara loved noisy cricket matches and Bholu loved quiet painting. Why is their friendship 'unlikely'?
qa.e: 'Unlikely' means not expected; their very different hobbies make the friendship surprising.

qa.q: What did Tara say at first about Bholu?
qa.e: Early in the story Tara grumbled, 'We have nothing in common.'

qa.q: Tara "grumbled" when she said they had nothing in common. 'Grumbled' means she spoke:
qa.e: To grumble is to complain in a low, unhappy voice.

qa.q: When Tara hurt her ankle, what did Bholu do?
qa.a: He taught her to paint the sunset
qa.e: Bholu came over with his paints and taught her to paint.

qa.q: Why did Tara cheer louder than anyone on Sports Day?
qa.a: Bholu was nervous and she wanted to support him
qa.e: The passage says Bholu was nervous before his race, so Tara supported him.

qa.q: Which word best describes Bholu when he visited Tara?
qa.e: Visiting a hurt friend and teaching her something new shows that he cares.

qa.q: What is the main idea of Tara and Bholu's story?
qa.a: Friends can be different and still care for each other
qa.e: The story shows two very different children becoming caring friends.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'unlikely'?
qa.e: Removing the prefix 'un-' gives 'likely', the opposite.

qa.q: What is an anecdote?
qa.a: A short, interesting story about a real person or event
qa.e: An anecdote is brief and about something that really happened (or is told as if it did).

qa.q: Anecdotes are usually told in which tense?
qa.e: They describe something that already happened, so they use the past tense.

qa.q: In the anecdote, Akbar asked his courtiers to make his line shorter. What was the tricky condition?
qa.a: They could not rub out any part of it
qa.e: The challenge was to shorten the line without erasing any part of it.

qa.q: How did Birbal solve the line puzzle?
qa.a: He drew a longer line beside it
qa.e: Next to a longer line, Akbar's line looked shorter.

qa.q: In the anecdote, "The courtiers were puzzled." 'Puzzled' means:
qa.e: To be puzzled is to be confused and unable to understand something.

qa.q: Which quality does the line anecdote show in Birbal?
qa.e: Wit means quick, clever thinking — exactly what Birbal showed.

qa.q: Who were Akbar's 'courtiers'?
qa.a: people who attended the emperor at his court
qa.e: A court is where a king or emperor met people; courtiers were the people there.

qa.q: Why might the friendship of an emperor and a courtier be called 'unlikely'?
qa.a: They were very different in position and power
qa.e: An emperor and a member of his court were very different in rank, so a close friendship would be surprising.

qa.q: Which is a proper noun?
qa.e: Agra names one particular city, so it is a proper noun.

qa.q: Which is an abstract noun?
qa.e: Friendship is a feeling or relationship we cannot touch.

qa.q: Fill in the collective noun: a ___ of bees.
qa.e: Bees fly in a swarm.

qa.q: Which is the abstract noun formed from 'brave'?
qa.e: Adding -ry gives the noun 'bravery'. 'Bravely' is an adverb.

qa.q: In 'The team won the match', what kind of noun is 'team'?
qa.e: 'Team' names a group of players as one unit.

qa.q: Which words need capital letters in: 'we visited the taj mahal in agra'?
qa.e: Proper nouns (Taj Mahal, Agra) and the first word of a sentence take capitals.

qa.q: What is the abstract noun formed from 'wise'?
qa.e: 'Wise' becomes 'wisdom'. 'Wisely' is an adverb and 'wiser' is a comparative.

qa.q: Which is a common noun?
qa.e: 'Girl' is a general name; the others are particular names (proper nouns).

qa.q: Read: "Let me be the friend who listens well, / Who keeps the secrets you choose to tell, / Who shares an umbrella when rain falls down, / And gently turns away your frown." What does the friend do when rain falls down?
qa.e: Line 3 says the friend shares an umbrella when rain falls down.

qa.q: In the poem, the friend "keeps the secrets you choose to tell". This shows the friend is:
qa.e: Keeping a friend's secrets shows you can be trusted.

qa.q: The poem's second stanza: "Let me be kind when you are wrong, / And help you up and make you strong; / For friendship isn't gold or gift — / It's a hand held out, a heart to lift." According to it, what is friendship?
qa.a: A hand held out and a heart to lift
qa.e: The last line says friendship is 'a hand held out, a heart to lift'.

qa.q: In the poem, "Let me be kind when you are wrong." What does the speaker promise?
qa.a: To be gentle even when the friend makes a mistake
qa.e: Being kind when someone is wrong means being gentle and forgiving.

qa.q: Which word in the poem rhymes with 'wrong'?
qa.e: 'Wrong' and 'strong' share the '-ong' sound.

qa.q: Why is the poem called a 'prayer'?
qa.a: It is a humble wish to be a good friend
qa.e: A prayer is a heartfelt wish or request; the poem wishes 'Let me be...' a good friend.

qa.q: What is the rhyme scheme of a stanza where lines 1 and 2 rhyme, and lines 3 and 4 rhyme?
qa.e: Matching letters show rhyming lines: first pair A A, second pair B B.

qa.q: Repeating 'Let me be' at the start of both stanzas is an example of:
qa.e: Using the same words again for effect is repetition.

qa.q: What is the noun form of 'kind'?
qa.e: Adding -ness to the adjective 'kind' makes the noun 'kindness'.

qa.q: The suffix '-less' means:
qa.e: -less means without: careless = without care.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'careful'?
qa.e: Careful (full of care) and careless (without care) are opposites.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'friendly'?
qa.e: The prefix un- means 'not': unfriendly. 'Friendless' means having no friends.

qa.q: Which is an act of kindness?
qa.a: Sharing your umbrella with a friend in the rain
qa.e: Sharing to help someone is kind.

qa.q: Fill in: Mohan was ___ to the old man and helped him cross the road.
qa.e: After 'was' we need an adjective; helping the old man shows he was kind.

qa.q: What does 'thankful' mean?
qa.e: -ful means 'full of', so thankful means full of thanks.

qa.q: What is the noun form of 'happy'?
qa.e: Change y to i and add -ness: happiness.

qa.q: Which word is a pronoun?
qa.e: 'They' replaces a plural noun, so it is a pronoun.

qa.q: Which sentence uses the subject pronoun correctly?
qa.a: Tara and I painted the sunset.
qa.e: The subject of the sentence needs the subject pronoun 'I'.

qa.q: Fill in: Mother gave ___ a hug.
qa.e: 'Us' is the object pronoun that receives the hug.

qa.q: Which is a reflexive pronoun?
qa.e: Reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'Is this umbrella ___?'
qa.e: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: yours.

qa.q: Which sentence uses 'its' correctly?
qa.e: 'Its' shows belonging; 'it's' means 'it is'.

qa.q: Replace the noun: 'Meena and Raju are friends. Meena and Raju study together.'
qa.e: Meena and Raju (subject, more than one person) → they.

qa.q: Fill in: 'The friends made a promise to ___ to be kind.'
qa.e: The correct reflexive form for 'the friends' is 'themselves'.

qa.q: Who is the narrator of the chair story?
qa.e: The story begins 'I am an old wooden chair', so the chair tells it.

qa.q: Where is the chair kept?
qa.e: The first line tells us the setting: Nani's verandah.

qa.q: In the story, "For forty years I have held tired visitors, giggling grandchildren and one very fat cat." What does this tell us?
qa.a: The chair is very old and has been used a lot
qa.e: Forty years of holding many people shows the chair is old and well used.

qa.q: "My legs creak now." Here the chair's 'legs' are:
qa.a: the wooden legs of the chair
qa.e: A chair has legs too — its wooden supports — and they creak because they are old.

qa.q: Which line shows personification?
qa.e: A chair cannot really feel; giving it feelings is personification.

qa.q: Why did Chintu call the chair 'my throne'?
qa.a: He loved it and imagined it as a king's seat
qa.e: Calling a painted old chair a throne shows love and imagination.

qa.q: The chair story is told in the:
qa.e: The narrator uses 'I', which is the first person.

qa.q: Which word best describes Chintu?
qa.e: He turned an old chair into a 'throne' in his mind and with paint.

qa.q: What is imagination?
qa.a: The power to picture ideas in your mind that are not really present
qa.e: Imagination lets us picture things that are not in front of us.

qa.q: Which word is the adjective meaning 'existing only in the mind, not real'?
qa.e: Something imaginary is not real; it exists only in the mind.

qa.q: Which sentence uses 'imaginative' correctly?
qa.a: Ravi is an imaginative boy who invents new games.
qa.e: Imaginative means creative, so it describes Ravi well. An unreal friend would be 'imaginary'.

qa.q: In a story, the 'setting' means:
qa.a: where and when the story happens
qa.e: The setting is the place and time of the story.

qa.q: What is the 'plot' of a story?
qa.a: the series of events that happen
qa.e: The plot is what happens in the story from start to end.

qa.q: Which is the best 'What if...?' story starter?
qa.a: What if my school bag could fly me to school?
qa.e: It asks an imaginative question that can lead to a fun story.
